newsitem.title: USA: New York officer fired on brutality charge.
newsitem.headline: New York officer fired on brutality charge.

text.p: New York's police chief Friday fired an officer involved in the choking death of a Bronx man, a case that has fuelled fears that the dramatic drop in crime has been accompanied by growing charges of police brutality.

Security guard Anthony Baez, 29, was playing a street football game with his brothers in Dec. 1994 when an altercation occurred with officer Francis Livoti, whose patrol car was struck twice by the ball.
A New York City Police Department Judge ruled two weeks ago that Livoti used an illegal choke hold in violation of police procedure to subdue Baez in a scuffle.

Livoti was acquitted of state criminal charges last year, a verdict that caused a brief, angry outburst inside and outside the courtroom by the Baez family and sympathisers. The family is suing Livoti in civil court for $48 million.

At a news conference announcing Livoti's dismissal, Police Commissioner Howard Safir said the officer had wrongfully applied the choke hold against Baez and that he had disregarded policy on the use of the choke hold.
Safir said Livoti's "inexplicable aggressiveness during what most reasonable officers understand to be a routine street encounter, escalated events into violence and a death resulted."
Livoti, 37, who worked 15 years as a police officer, would have become eligible for a pension next week, but has now lost the annual $17,600 that would have been due to him starting in 2003.
Livoti and his lawyer could not be immediately reached for comment on his dismissal.
Safir, defending his department against charges of brutality, described it as "a wrong perception" but would "certainly not pretend that there are not others out there who might act inappropriately."
He vowed to act against officers who abuse their authority and said those with a record of complaints against them were being more closely monitored.

As the rate of serious crime plummeted in recent years to the lowest levels in almost a generation, reports of alleged police brutality increased, particularly where minorities were involved, according to a report last June by the human rights group Amnesty International.
The city's own Civilian Complaint Review also reported an increase in alleged abuses last year.
"This department is not a brutal department," Safir said Friday. "I will not tolerate brutality on the part of any police officer or any other employee."

An opinion poll for the NY1 News local TV channel released this week revealed that most New York City voters think police brutality is a serious problem and that police do not treat different ethnic groups even-handedly.

The poll, taken Feb. 2-6, found that 81 percent of blacks and 73 percent of Hispanics think police brutality is a serious problem in the city. The poll of 1,202 registered voters has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percent.
